question: In France, as in several Member States, local councils are reporting an increase in damage to places of worship and religious reflection, such as wayside crosses, statues, chapels and memorial caves. Such sites play a vital role in local memory and identity in rural areas.

Recently, vandals wrecked the Libaux cave in Lessard-en-Bresse (Saône-et-Loire), a replica of the cave at Lourdes built after the Second World War. Statuettes were decapitated, the altar was destroyed and panels were smashed. This is the third time in 10 years that the cave has been vandalised.

In small communities, such sites are principally restored and looked after by volunteers, and security measures are often too expensive. These events show that religious heritage is under threat in many parts of Europe. 1.

Is the Commission planning to make instruments available that will make it possible to help rural municipalities deal with repeated damage to their religious heritage, in particular with a view to restoring and securing the sites concerned?
Could the creation of a specific budget heading for the protection and restoration of religious heritage in rural areas be considered?
Supporters1
This question is supported by Members other than the authors: Julien Leonardelli (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.3.2026) The EU action in the field of culture aims to encourage cooperation between Member States, and to support and supplement their actions, including on the conservation and safeguarding of cultural heritage, in line with Article 167 of the Treaty of the Functioning of the EU. Management of cultural heritage remains primarily a national responsibility.

In the 2021–2027 programming period, the restoration, preservation and enhancement of cultural heritage, including religious, is eligible for support under the European Regional Development Fund. The Fund has already supported religious heritage restoration projects, when linked with local development, social cohesion or the attractiveness of rural areas.
The responsibility for the selection of operations lies with the managing authorities, such as the Regional Councils in the case of France.

The Commission's proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 is built on an integrated and flexible delivery model centred on national and regional partnership plans, where Member States and regions have greater flexibility in allocating resources to address local development needs, including religious heritage.
